entities.label: Waived SAP Notification Group
entities.sub: 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) - the chairman and ranking minority member of each defense committee; twelve members, not the Gang of Eight
entities.desc: The group that receives notification of a WAIVED Department of Defense special access program is not the Gang of Eight, and conflating the two is the single most common error in public argument about how a legacy programme could be hidden. The waived-SAP channel is created by 10 U.S.C. 119(e). Subsection (e)(1) provides: 'The Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis.' Subsection (e)(2) then specifies where the withheld material goes instead: 'If the Secretary exercises the authority provided under paragraph (1), the Secretary shall provide the information described in that subsection with respect to the special access program concerned, and the justification for the waiver, jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.' The term 'defense committees' is defined not by the general Title 10 definition but by section 119's own subsection (g): 'the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations, and the Defense Subcommittee of the Committee on Appropriations, of the Senate' and 'the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations, and the Subcommittee on Defense of the Committee on Appropriations, of the House of Representatives.' Six bodies, each contributing a chairman and a ranking minority member: twelve members of Congress. This is deliberately narrower than a full committee and deliberately wider than eight. Note that 10 U.S.C. 101(a)(16) defines a different, similar-sounding term, 'congressional defense committees,' as only the Armed Services and Appropriations Committees of the two chambers - four bodies, eight chairs and rankings. Section 119 does not use that definition; it uses its own, which adds the two Defense Appropriations Subcommittees. A board that cites 101(a)(16) for the waived-SAP group would be naming the wrong set. The Gang of Eight is a separate creature governing covert action, not DoD SAPs. Under 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(2), where the President determines that it is essential to limit access to a covert action finding to meet extraordinary circumstances affecting vital interests of the United States, 'the finding may be reported to the chairmen and ranking minority members of the congressional intelligence committees, the Speaker and minority leader of the House of Representatives, the majority and minority leaders of the Senate, and such other member or members of the congressional leadership as may be included by the President.' Different committees (intelligence, not armed services or appropriations), different people (the four party leaders sit in the Gang of Eight and are absent from the 119(e) group; the appropriators sit in the 119(e) group and are absent from the Gang of Eight), and different subject matter. The structural comparison is where the argument actually lives, and it cuts against the covert-action statute being the tighter one. Title 50 contains two escape valves that Title 10 does not. First, 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(5)(B) imposes a 180-day clock: within 180 days of a statement of reasons for limiting access, the President must either give all members of the intelligence committees access to the finding or submit a fresh statement of reasons for continuing to withhold. Section 119(e) contains no sunset, no periodic re-justification, and no mechanism that ever widens the circle. A waiver, once made, is permanent as to that report. Second, 50 U.S.C. 3093(g)(1)-(2) requires the President to tell all members of the intelligence committee that a limited notification occurred and to give them a general description of it. Section 119 has no analogue: the members of the Armed Services and Appropriations Committees who are not chair or ranking are never told that a waiver happened at all. They cannot ask about what they do not know exists. That asymmetry - no sunset, no notice of bypass - is the load-bearing limit on congressional oversight of a waived programme, and it is a limit written into the statute rather than an abuse of it. What the twelve can see is also bounded. They receive the withheld report content and the Secretary's justification. They do not thereby acquire subpoena power over the programme, staff who can read the material, or any statutory right to share it with colleagues. What they cannot see is anything the Department declines to characterise as a DoD special access program at all - the recurring allegation in the UAP context being that recovery and reverse-engineering activity was moved into contractor-held or non-DoD structures where section 119 does not reach. Finally, the mechanism's present scope is narrower than it was. Pub. L. 114-328 section 1061(c)(4) lists 'Section 119(a) and (b)' among the reporting requirements it terminates, and section 1061(b)(1) provides that each such report still required as of December 31, 2021 'shall no longer be required to be submitted to Congress after that date.' The Office of the Law Revision Counsel carries this as a Termination of Reporting Requirements note under section 119. The annual SAP budget report and the annual new-SAP designation-and-justification report are therefore gone. Because 119(e)(1) can only waive a requirement 'under subsection (a), (b), or (c),' the waiver authority now has live operation only as to subsection (c), the report on a planned change in classification or a planned declassification and public announcement. Subsections (d), (f) and (g) survive and are not waivable at all - notably 119(f), which bars initiating any SAP until the defense committees are notified and thirty days elapse.

claims.text: 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) directs waived-SAP information and the waiver justification 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' - twelve members, given the six bodies listed in 119(g).

10 U.S.C. 119(g) defines 'defense committees' for this section as the Senate Armed Services Committee, Senate Appropriations Committee, Senate Appropriations Defense Subcommittee, House Armed Services Committee, House Appropriations Committee, and House Appropriations Defense Subcommittee.

10 U.S.C. 101(a)(16) defines the different term 'congressional defense committees' as only '(A) the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations of the Senate; and (B) the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations of the House of Representatives' - four bodies, not the six used by section 119.

The Gang of Eight under 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(2) consists of 'the chairmen and ranking minority members of the congressional intelligence committees, the Speaker and minority leader of the House of Representatives, the majority and minority leaders of the Senate, and such other member or members of the congressional leadership as may be included by the President.' It governs covert action findings, not DoD special access programs.

50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(5)(B) forces re-justification or widened access within 180 days of a limited covert-action notification. 10 U.S.C. 119(e) contains no sunset and no re-justification requirement, so a SAP reporting waiver is permanent as to that report.

50 U.S.C. 3093(g)(1)-(2) requires that all members of the intelligence committee be told a limited notification occurred and be given a general description of it. Section 119 imposes no equivalent duty, so non-leadership members of the defense committees are never informed that a waiver has been exercised.

Pub. L. 114-328 sec. 1061(c)(4) lists 'Section 119(a) and (b)' among terminated reporting requirements, and sec. 1061(b)(1) ends them after 31 December 2021. The OLRC note under section 119 records the termination as effective 31 December 2021.

Because 119(e)(1) reaches only 'a requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c),' and (a) and (b) terminated on 31 December 2021, the waiver authority retains live operation only as to subsection (c) - reports of a planned classification change or declassification. This is an inference from the statutory text, not a statement carried in the statute itself.

10 U.S.C. 119(f) bars initiating a special access program until the defense committees are notified and thirty days elapse. Subsection (f) is outside the reach of the 119(e)(1) waiver, which by its terms covers only subsections (a), (b) and (c).

DoD Directive 5205.07, reissued 12 September 2024, sets DoD special access program policy and its glossary defines SAP, SAP umbrella, SAP compartment, Joint Force Integration SAP and Strategic Enabler SAP. It does not define or use the terms 'acknowledged', 'unacknowledged' or 'waived' SAP, which appeared in the superseded July 2010 version.

DoDD 5205.07 para. 3.1.g requires all personnel accessed to DoD SAPs to notify the Director, DoD SAPCO through their cognizant authority SAPCO when briefing or providing DoD SAP material to any member of Congress or their staff, and bars any DoD contractor entity, employee, representative or consultant from providing SAP material to members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval.
DoDD 5205.07 para. 2.1.e assigns the Director, DoD SAPCO responsibility to accredit congressional SAP facilities and to maintain records of DoD SAP information provided to Congress.

people.label: Roger F. Wicker
people.sub: Chairman, Senate Armed Services Committee (119th Congress, serving August 2026); Ranking Member of the same committee in the 118th Congress, including 2023
people.narrative: Wicker holds the senior of the twelve seats that 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) designates. As chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee he is entitled, jointly with his ranking member, to receive any special access program information the Secretary of Defense withholds from a section 119 report under the waiver authority, together with the Secretary's written justification for withholding it. He is also among the members entitled to the notification required by 119(f) before any SAP may be initiated, and to the classification-change reports required by 119(c) - the one category of report to which the waiver still attaches after the 2021 termination of subsections (a) and (b). Wicker is on the board for a structural reason rather than a UAP-specific one, and the absence of a UAP record is itself the point: he occupies one of only twelve offices in the United States government with a statutory entitlement to see inside a waived DoD special access program, and there is no public record of him having stated what he has or has not been shown. He was in the same twelve-member set during the 118th Congress, when he sat as ranking member opposite Jack Reed - meaning he held a 119(e)(2) seat at the time of the July 2023 Grusch testimony before the House Oversight Committee, a committee that has no entitlement under section 119 at all. His continuity across both configurations, ranking member then chairman, makes him the longest-serving current occupant of a 119(e)(2) seat on the Senate armed services side.

people.label: Jack Reed
people.sub: Ranking Member, Senate Armed Services Committee (119th Congress, serving August 2026); Chairman in the 118th Congress including 2023; Ranking Member in the 116th Congress including 2020
people.narrative: Reed is the single most continuously entitled person on this board. He has held a 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) seat on the Senate Armed Services Committee across every one of the load-bearing moments the board tracks after 2009: he was ranking member in 2020 when the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force was stood up, chairman in 2023 when David Grusch testified, and ranking member again in August 2026. In each configuration he was entitled to receive waived special access program information and the Secretary's justification for the waiver, jointly with his opposite number. He also sits on the Senate Appropriations Committee and its Defense Subcommittee, though membership on those bodies confers nothing under section 119 - only the chair and ranking seats do. Reed's importance to the board is that he is the continuity: where chairmanships rotated with party control, Reed occupied one of the two Senate armed services seats without interruption. If a waived DoD special access program concerning recovered non-human technology existed and was notified under 119(e)(2) at any point between 2015 and 2026, Reed is the person most likely to have received that notification. He has made no public statement to that effect, and no public statement denying it. That silence is the expected behaviour of someone lawfully constrained by the statute, and it is not evidence either way - but it does mean the board should treat him as a node of known entitlement rather than known knowledge.

people.label: Susan M. Collins
people.sub: Chair, Senate Appropriations Committee (119th Congress, serving August 2026); Ranking Member of that committee and of its Defense Subcommittee in the 118th Congress including 2023
people.narrative: Collins occupies the Senate Appropriations chair, one of the six chairmanships that generate a 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) entitlement. Her presence in the group illustrates why the Gang of Eight comparison misleads: appropriators are inside the waived-SAP circle and outside the covert-action circle, while the party leaders are the reverse. Collins is the money side of the entitlement. A waived special access program still has to be paid for, and the appropriations leadership sees the classified annex material that the authorising committees do not necessarily see in the same form. In 2023 Collins held two of the twelve seats simultaneously - ranking member of the full Appropriations Committee and ranking member of its Defense Subcommittee - which is a recurring feature of the group worth flagging: because the same senator often occupies both the full-committee and subcommittee seat, the twelve statutory seats are frequently filled by fewer than twelve distinct people. In the 118th Congress the Senate side of the 119(e)(2) group comprised only five individuals rather than six for exactly this reason. Collins has no publicly documented UAP-specific record. As with the other holders, the absence is notable rather than exculpatory: the statute gives her sight of waived programme material and gives her no mechanism to disclose it.

people.label: Patty Murray
people.sub: Vice Chair, Senate Appropriations Committee (119th Congress, serving August 2026); Chairman of that committee in the 118th Congress including 2023
people.narrative: Murray holds the ranking minority position on the Senate Appropriations Committee, which that committee styles Vice Chair rather than Ranking Member. The title difference does not affect the statutory entitlement: 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) speaks of 'the ranking minority member of each of the defense committees,' and Murray is the senior member of the minority on the Senate Appropriations Committee, so the waived-SAP notification runs to her jointly with Chair Collins. A board rendering the group should be careful not to omit her on the ground that the Senate Appropriations minority leader is not called a ranking member. Murray and Collins have traded the chair and vice chair positions between the 118th and 119th Congresses, so both have held a 119(e)(2) seat continuously since at least January 2023 - Murray as chairman in 2023, vice chair thereafter. That means Murray held a seat entitling her to waived special access program notification at the time of the July 2023 Grusch testimony and at the time of the fiscal 2024 Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act debate. She has no publicly documented UAP-specific record, and her committee has no public UAP jurisdiction, but the appropriations channel is where a waived programme's funding would necessarily surface in some form.

people.label: Mitch McConnell
people.sub: Chair, Defense Subcommittee of the Senate Appropriations Committee (119th Congress, serving August 2026)
people.narrative: McConnell chairs the Senate Appropriations Defense Subcommittee, a body that 10 U.S.C. 119(g)(1) names explicitly as one of the six defense committees. This is the seat that distinguishes the section 119 group from the 10 U.S.C. 101(a)(16) definition of congressional defense committees, which does not reach the Defense Subcommittees. McConnell is in the waived-SAP circle because section 119 uses its own broader definition. McConnell is also the clearest illustration of how the two small groups diverge over time for the same person. As Senate majority leader and later minority leader he was a member of the Gang of Eight under 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(2) by virtue of his leadership office, seeing covert action findings the armed services committees never saw. He now sits in the 119(e)(2) group by virtue of a subcommittee gavel, seeing waived DoD special access program material that the intelligence committees have no statutory entitlement to. The two entitlements are disjoint and neither implies the other. For a board arguing that a waived programme can be concealed from Congress, McConnell is the counter-example worth naming: a single member who has occupied seats in both restricted-notification regimes, and whose combined sight lines are still bounded by whether the activity in question was characterised as a DoD special access program at all.

claims.text: Mitch McConnell (R-KY) is listed as Chair of the Defense Subcommittee of the Senate Appropriations Committee on the subcommittee's official page.

The Defense Subcommittee of the Senate Committee on Appropriations is one of the six bodies expressly named as a 'defense committee' by 10 U.S.C. 119(g)(1), and therefore generates a 119(e)(2) notification entitlement for its chair and ranking minority member.

people.label: Christopher A. Coons
people.sub: Ranking Member, Defense Subcommittee of the Senate Appropriations Committee (119th Congress, serving August 2026)
people.narrative: Coons is the ranking minority member of the Senate Appropriations Defense Subcommittee and therefore the twelfth-listed of the twelve statutory recipients on the Senate side. His entitlement under 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) is identical in scope to the chairman's: the withheld report information and the Secretary of Defense's justification for the waiver go to chair and ranking jointly, not to the chair alone. The joint character of the notification is a deliberate anti-capture feature of the statute and should be represented on the board as such - a waived-SAP notification cannot lawfully be given to one party's leadership only. What Coons does not have is any statutory right to widen the circle. Nothing in section 119 permits him to brief the rest of his subcommittee, and unlike his counterparts on the intelligence committees under 50 U.S.C. 3093(g), he has no assurance that his non-leadership colleagues will even be told that a limited notification occurred. Coons has no publicly documented UAP-specific record. His subcommittee's jurisdiction, as published by the Senate Appropriations Committee, extends across the Central Intelligence Agency, the National Reconnaissance Office, the National Security Agency, the Defense Intelligence Agency and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency in addition to the military departments, which makes the Defense Subcommittee seats unusually broad in practice relative to their narrow statutory description.

claims.text: Christopher A. Coons (D-DE) is listed as Ranking Member of the Defense Subcommittee of the Senate Appropriations Committee on the subcommittee's official page.

The published jurisdiction of the Senate Appropriations Defense Subcommittee includes the Central Intelligence Agency, the Defense Intelligence Agency, the National Reconnaissance Office, the National Security Agency and the National Geospatial and Intelligence Agency alongside the military departments.

people.label: Mike Rogers (Alabama)
people.sub: Chairman, House Armed Services Committee (118th and 119th Congresses, serving August 2026)
people.narrative: Rogers has chaired the House Armed Services Committee since the start of the 118th Congress and holds that chair in August 2026, which places him in the 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) group continuously across the 2023 Grusch testimony and everything since. He must be distinguished on the board from Mike Rogers of Michigan, a different member who chaired the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence - a committee with no entitlement whatsoever under section 119. Conflating the two would put the wrong person in the group and attach the wrong committee to the wrong statute. The Rogers seat is the House authorising counterpart to Wicker's. It carries the same joint entitlement with the ranking member to receive waived special access program information and the waiver justification, the same 119(f) thirty-day pre-initiation notification, and the same absence of any statutory route to share what is received. Rogers's committee is also the vehicle through which the annual National Defense Authorization Act and its classified annex are produced, which is the practical mechanism by which Congress has repeatedly attempted to legislate visibility into UAP-related programmes. That gives the House Armed Services chairmanship a dual character on this board: a statutory recipient seat under section 119, and the drafting seat for the legislation that has sought to widen section 119-style access.

people.label: Adam Smith
people.sub: Ranking Member, House Armed Services Committee (118th and 119th Congresses, serving August 2026); Chairman of the same committee in the 116th Congress including 2020
people.narrative: Smith is the House-side equivalent of Jack Reed: the member whose occupancy of a 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) seat spans the board's load-bearing moments regardless of which party held the House. He chaired the House Armed Services Committee in 2020, when the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force was established, and has been its ranking member throughout the 118th and 119th Congresses, covering the 2023 Grusch testimony and the period since. In every one of those configurations he was one of the twelve members entitled to receive waived special access program information and the Secretary of Defense's justification for withholding it from a section 119 report. Smith's continuity matters for the board's central argument. The claim that a waived unacknowledged programme can be concealed from Congress because notification runs to only a handful of members is testable in part against whether those handful of members have been stable over time. On the armed services side they have been remarkably stable: Reed and Smith between them have held a 119(e)(2) seat without interruption across three Congresses in which control of both chambers changed. There is no public record of Smith stating what he has or has not been notified of under section 119. The statute gives him no route to make such a statement.

people.label: Tom Cole
people.sub: Chairman, House Appropriations Committee (119th Congress, serving as of June 2026)
people.narrative: Cole chairs the House Appropriations Committee and therefore holds one of the twelve seats designated by 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2). The House Appropriations chairmanship is the House counterpart to Collins's Senate seat, and it carries the same feature that makes the appropriations pair distinctive within the group: appropriators see the money before they see the programme description. A waived special access program whose reporting content has been withheld under 119(e)(1) is nonetheless funded through bills that Cole's committee writes, and through classified annexes that his committee produces. Cole was confirmed in the chair as of June 2026, issuing a joint statement with Defense Subcommittee Chairman Ken Calvert on the administration's defense supplemental request. On the board he should be treated as a current-entitlement node rather than a historical one: his tenure in the 119(e)(2) group begins after all three of the load-bearing moments the board tracks, so he has no 2009, 2020 or 2023 role in this group. He has no publicly documented UAP-specific record. The value of naming him is completeness of the set - the argument that only a handful of members receive waived-SAP notification is only as strong as the board's ability to name the handful correctly and currently.

people.label: Rosa L. DeLauro
people.sub: Ranking Member, House Appropriations Committee (118th and 119th Congresses, serving August 2026)
people.narrative: DeLauro has been the ranking minority member of the House Appropriations Committee across the 118th and 119th Congresses, which places her in the 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) group continuously from January 2023 through August 2026, including the period of the July 2023 Grusch testimony. Her seat is one of the four appropriations seats in the group - full committee chair and ranking in each chamber - that have no analogue in the Gang of Eight. She was ranking member opposite Chairwoman Kay Granger in the 118th Congress and opposite Chairman Tom Cole in the 119th. Her continuity through a change of chairman is the House appropriations equivalent of the Reed and Smith pattern on the armed services side. DeLauro has no publicly documented UAP-specific record. Her entitlement under section 119 is to receive, jointly with the chairman, whatever the Secretary of Defense withholds from a section 119 report plus the justification for the waiver. As with every other member of the group, that entitlement comes with no staff-sharing right, no disclosure route, and no sunset that would eventually force the material into wider committee view. In the intelligence context an equivalent limitation would expire after 180 days under 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(5)(B). In the DoD SAP context it does not expire at all.

people.label: Ken Calvert
people.sub: Chair, Defense Subcommittee of the House Appropriations Committee (118th and 119th Congresses, serving August 2026); Ranking Member of the same subcommittee in the 116th Congress including 2020
people.narrative: Calvert is the third member of the twelve whose occupancy spans multiple load-bearing moments. He was the ranking minority member of the House Appropriations Defense Subcommittee in 2020, when Peter J. Visclosky chaired it and the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force was established, and he has chaired that subcommittee across the 118th and 119th Congresses, covering the 2023 Grusch testimony and the period through August 2026. In both roles he has held a 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) seat. The House Appropriations Defense Subcommittee is named expressly in 10 U.S.C. 119(g)(2) and its published jurisdiction runs to the Central Intelligence Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence in addition to the military departments and defense agencies. That makes the subcommittee chair one of the few offices in Congress that combines a statutory waived-SAP entitlement with appropriations reach across both the defense and intelligence budgets. Calvert has no publicly documented UAP-specific record. On the board he is the strongest single candidate for the proposition that a small number of members have had sustained, lawful, multi-year sight of whatever waived DoD special access program material the Department has chosen to route through 119(e)(2) - and equally the strongest illustration that such sight produces no public trace, because the statute provides none.

people.label: Betty McCollum
people.sub: Ranking Member, Defense Subcommittee of the House Appropriations Committee (118th and 119th Congresses, serving August 2026)
people.narrative: McCollum is the ranking minority member of the House Appropriations Defense Subcommittee and has held that seat across the 118th and 119th Congresses, placing her in the 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) group from January 2023 through August 2026, including the July 2023 Grusch testimony. She sat on the same subcommittee as vice chair in the 116th Congress in 2020, but the vice chair seat is not one of the twelve - only the chair and the ranking minority member are named by section 119(e)(2), and in 2020 those were Visclosky and Calvert. That distinction is worth preserving on the board, because it is exactly the kind of near-miss that produces incorrect membership lists: sitting on a defense committee, even in a leadership-adjacent role, confers nothing under section 119. McCollum's current seat completes the House side of the group. Her subcommittee's jurisdiction, as published, includes the Central Intelligence Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. She has no publicly documented UAP-specific record. Her position is the House minority's only statutory window into a waived DoD special access program on the appropriations side, and the statute gives her no means of using it beyond her own knowledge - no right to brief her caucus, no right to inform the rest of her subcommittee, and no clock that eventually forces disclosure to them.

edges.label: created by 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) and defined by 119(g)
edges.note: Section 119 was added by Pub. L. 100-180 div. A title XI sec. 1132(a)(1), 4 December 1987. Subsection (e)(2) directs waived-SAP information and the waiver justification jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each defense committee; subsection (g) supplies the six-body definition of 'defense committees' used by the section.

edges.label: sole statutory recipient of waived-SAP notification
edges.note: The waiver mechanism at 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1) does not eliminate reporting; it redirects it. Whatever the Secretary withholds from the report goes instead to these twelve members under 119(e)(2), together with the justification for withholding.

edges.label: the twelve members with statutory sight of a waived programme
edges.note: Entitlement is bounded by characterisation: section 119 reaches only activity the Department treats as a DoD special access program. Activity held outside that characterisation is outside the group's statutory sight line entirely.

edges.label: the narrow aperture through which Congress sees waived DoD SAPs
edges.note: Section 119 contains no analogue to 50 U.S.C. 3093(g), which requires that the rest of the committee be told a limited notification occurred. Members of the defense committees outside the twelve are not informed that a waiver has been exercised.

edges.label: one of the six defense committees named in 10 U.S.C. 119(g)(1)
edges.note: Contributes two of the twelve seats: the chairman and the ranking minority member. Ordinary committee membership confers no entitlement.

edges.label: not a defense committee; receives nothing under 10 U.S.C. 119
edges.note: The July 2023 Grusch testimony was taken by a House Oversight subcommittee. That committee has no entitlement under section 119(e)(2) and no statutory route to compel waived-SAP material, which is a structural reason why the hearing could establish allegation but not access.

edges.label: accredits congressional SAP facilities and records SAP information given to Congress
edges.note: DoDD 5205.07 para. 2.1.e assigns the Director, DoD SAPCO responsibility to accredit congressional SAPFs and maintain records of DoD SAP information provided to Congress. Para. 2.1.a(5) makes the Director the DoD primary point of contact for SAP matters with the Legislative Branch.

edges.label: contractor disclosure to Congress requires SAPCO approval
edges.note: DoDD 5205.07 para. 3.1.g bars any DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative or consultant from providing SAP material to any member of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval, and requires all accessed personnel to notify SAPCO when briefing Congress.

edges.label: Secretary of Defense is the notifying authority under 119(e)
edges.note: The waiver decision under 119(e)(1) belongs to the Secretary of Defense personally and must be made case by case on a determination that inclusion would adversely affect the national security. The statute prescribes no review of that determination.

edges.label: four of the twelve seats are appropriations leadership
edges.note: The chair and ranking of both Appropriations Committees and both Defense Subcommittees sit in the 119(e)(2) group. This is the structural feature that distinguishes it from the Gang of Eight, which contains no appropriators, and it means the group's sight of a waived programme includes the money as well as the report.

edges.label: Senate Majority Leader in 2009 - in the Gang of Eight, not in the 119(e)(2) group
edges.note: This is the cleanest demonstration that the two small groups are different sets. 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(2) includes the majority and minority leaders of the Senate. 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) and 119(g) do not; they reach only committee and subcommittee chairs and ranking members. A Senate Majority Leader has no statutory entitlement to waived DoD SAP notification by virtue of that office. In 2009 the Senate armed services and appropriations seats were held by Levin, McCain, Inouye and Cochran.

edges.label: allegations of a programme withheld from the statutory notification channel
edges.note: Grusch's 26 July 2023 testimony was given to a House Oversight subcommittee, which holds no entitlement under section 119. The twelve members who did hold 119(e)(2) seats on that date were Reed, Wicker, Murray, Collins, Tester, Rogers of Alabama, Smith, Granger, DeLauro, Calvert and McCollum - eleven distinct individuals, because Collins held both Senate appropriations seats. None has made a public statement about what, if anything, was notified to them under section 119.

edges.label: House Armed Services member but not chair or ranking - no 119(e)(2) entitlement
edges.note: Mace sits on the House Armed Services Committee, one of the six defense committees, yet receives nothing under section 119(e)(2), which names only the chairman and ranking minority member. She would also not be told under section 119 that a waiver had been exercised at all. This is the clearest single illustration of how narrow the aperture is even inside a defense committee.

edges.label: no statutory entitlement; not a defense committee chair or ranking member
edges.note: Burlison is not listed among the members of the House Armed Services Committee and does not hold a chair or ranking seat on any of the six bodies named in 10 U.S.C. 119(g). His UAP oversight work therefore proceeds without any section 119 entitlement.

edges.note: Luna is not listed among the members of the House Armed Services Committee and does not hold a chair or ranking seat on any of the six bodies named in 10 U.S.C. 119(g).

edges.label: caucus membership confers no statutory access
edges.note: A congressional caucus is not a committee and appears nowhere in 10 U.S.C. 119(g). Caucus members acquire no entitlement to waived-SAP notification, which is why UAP advocacy in Congress has consistently sought to legislate new access rather than to invoke existing access.

findings: The board's premise needs correcting in a specific way. Waived DoD special access programs are not governed by the Gang of Eight at all. They are governed by 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2), which routes withheld information to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of six bodies - twelve seats, not eight - and those six bodies are defined by section 119's own subsection (g), not by the general Title 10 definition at 101(a)(16). Getting this wrong in either direction (naming the party leaders, or dropping the two Defense Appropriations Subcommittees) produces the wrong set.

The genuinely surprising result concerns the post-2021 status. Pub. L. 114-328 sec. 1061(c)(4) expressly lists 'Section 119(a) and (b)' among terminated reporting requirements, and sec. 1061(b)(1) ends them after 31 December 2021. The Office of the Law Revision Counsel carries this as a Termination of Reporting Requirements note under section 119. Because 119(e)(1) can only waive 'any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c),' and two of those three subsections no longer generate reports, the waiver authority now has live operation only as to subsection (c) - the report of a planned classification change or declassification. In short: the annual SAP budget report and the annual new-SAP designation-and-justification report that the waiver was principally designed to hollow out no longer exist. The waiver mechanism survives, but there is far less left for it to waive.

The 30-day pre-initiation notification at 10 U.S.C. 119(f) is not waivable. Subsection (e)(1) by its terms reaches only subsections (a), (b) and (c). So even for a waived programme, the statute requires that the full defense committees - not just the twelve - be notified before the programme is initiated and that thirty days elapse. If a legacy recovery and reverse-engineering programme has never been notified under 119(f), the concealment cannot be attributed to the waiver mechanism; it would have to be attributed to the programme never having been characterised as a DoD special access program in the first place, or to predating the 1987 enactment.

The waived-SAP channel is in two identifiable respects weaker than the covert-action channel it is usually compared to. 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(5)(B) forces the President either to widen access to all members of the intelligence committees or to submit a fresh statement of reasons every 180 days. Section 119 has no sunset and no re-justification requirement at all - a waiver, once made, is permanent as to that report. And 50 U.S.C. 3093(g)(1)-(2) requires the President to tell the rest of the intelligence committee that a limited notification occurred and to give a general description of it; section 119 imposes no such duty, so the non-leadership members of the Armed Services and Appropriations Committees are never even told that a waiver has been exercised. On both counts the DoD SAP regime is the more opaque of the two.

DoD's own vocabulary has moved. DoD Directive 5205.07 was reissued on 12 September 2024, superseding the July 2010 version, and its glossary does not define or use the terms 'acknowledged', 'unacknowledged' or 'waived' SAP. The new taxonomy is SAP umbrellas, compartments and sub-compartments, split between 'Joint Force Integration SAPs' and 'Strategic Enabler SAPs'. The statutory waiver at 10 U.S.C. 119(e) is unaffected, but boards and reporting that use 'waived SAP' as if it were current DoD terminology are using a category that the governing directive no longer names.

The same reissued directive contains a provision directly relevant to the whistleblower question: DoDD 5205.07 para. 3.1.g bars any DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative or consultant from providing SAP material to any member of Congress or their staff without the approval of the Director, DoD SAPCO, and requires all accessed personnel to notify SAPCO whenever they brief or provide SAP material to a member of Congress or staff. Para. 2.1.e makes the Director responsible for accrediting congressional SAP facilities and for maintaining the records of DoD SAP information provided to Congress. The chokepoint for congressional access to SAP material is therefore a single DoD office reporting directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense.

Because the same member often holds both the full-committee and the subcommittee seat, the twelve statutory seats are frequently filled by fewer than twelve people. In the 118th Congress, Susan Collins held both Senate appropriations seats, so on the date of the Grusch testimony the group comprised eleven distinct individuals occupying twelve seats.

Three members have held a 119(e)(2) seat across multiple load-bearing moments regardless of which party controlled the chamber: Jack Reed (Senate Armed Services, 2020 and 2023 and 2026), Adam Smith (House Armed Services, 2020 and 2023 and 2026) and Ken Calvert (House Appropriations Defense Subcommittee, 2020 and 2023 and 2026). If any waived-SAP notification concerning UAP-related activity was made between 2020 and 2026, these three are the members most likely to have received it in every instance.

Nancy Mace sits on the House Armed Services Committee but is not its chairman or ranking member, and therefore receives nothing under 119(e)(2) and would not be told a waiver had occurred. She is on the board already, which makes her a useful on-board illustration of how narrow the aperture is even inside a named defense committee.
unresolved: Whether the Department of Defense continues in practice to provide SAP budget and new-programme information to the defense committees after the 31 December 2021 termination of 10 U.S.C. 119(a) and (b) - for example under classified annex direction in annual authorisation or appropriations acts, or voluntarily - and whether the 119(e)(2) chair-and-ranking channel is still used for that material. This could not be established from statutory text and would require the classified annex language or committee report language to resolve.

Whether any waiver under 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1) has ever been exercised in connection with UAP-related activity. No public record establishes this either way, and the statute creates no public reporting of the fact that a waiver occurred.

The precise date on which Howard P. 'Buck' McKeon replaced John M. McHugh as the senior Republican on the House Armed Services Committee in 2009. The December 2009 Congressional Directory shows McKeon in the seat and army.mil records McHugh taking office as Secretary of the Army in 2009, but the exact date of the House Armed Services succession was not confirmed from a primary source. For any claim tied to a specific 2009 date, verify which of the two held the ranking seat on that date.

The name of the 2009 Senate Appropriations Defense Subcommittee ranking minority member is taken from the first-listed Republican in the 111th Congress committee assignment publication rather than from an explicit 'ranking member' designation. The publication marks chairmen explicitly but identifies minority seniority only by list order. The reading is that Thad Cochran held it, consistent with his position as the full committee's senior Republican, but the publication does not label it.

Whether the September 2024 reissuance of DoDD 5205.07 formally retired the acknowledged / unacknowledged / waived taxonomy or merely omitted it from the directive while retaining it in the subordinate instruction DoDI 5205.11, which was reissued the same day and was not retrieved. This matters for how the board should label the waived-usap node.
Whether Tom Cole's tenure as House Appropriations chairman began before the 119th Congress. The sources retrieved confirm him in the chair as of June 2026 but do not establish a start date.
